I feel like Dumbledore was in a difficult situation, and as such I can't really blame him for what he did. What I loved about the seventh book is that JK Rowling revealed Dumbledore to be a man with flaws and all, as opposed to the all-knowing perfect person that he comes across as in earlier books.

Basically I guess after the final book, I decided that yes, Dumbledore was flawed, but still, as Hagrid would say: "Great man, Dumbledore." :)

He's simply human. Flawed, and certainly not beyond making mistakes, but he understood the cause for the greater good. He made the difficult choices that others may not have been able to take, knowing the self-sacrifices that had to be made.

Was it all selfless? No, not really. As we saw with the ring he allowed his emotions and want to see his deceased loved ones to cloud rational judgement.

He also could have done something about Voldemort before he became the souless being that he was, but I believed he tried to see something good and hoped that Voldemort would change his ways. Who knows for sure what was going through his mind with that.

He was a great man, but he was still just a man.

On the other hand though, Harry's willingness to sacrifice himself had to be a choice that he made on his own. If not, the magic would not have worked the way it was supposed to in order to destroy the horcrux within him and protect those he cared about. Love is a very powerful magic after all. If it were done out of selfish reasons, it simply wouldn't have been as strong, if it worked at all. Hence why it had to be selfless.

I feel like Dumbledore really knew all along that there was a chance Harry would live through the killing curse a second time and that the horcrux within him would die. After reading the 7th book, my opinion on Dumbledore did not really change- I still saw him as a great man who looked at the big picture.

Ex-radio employee here. I can't speak for the larger news agencies, but give the small, local companies in your area a chance. They don't always have the best material to work with (if you've ever wondered they cover so many shootings/random crimes at night, that's because there seriously isn't anything else going on in the area; they don't like it either. The stations that try to sensationalize it are definitely frowned upon too. Thankfully, that's less common in radio then in TV), but they seriously do work hard to get things right.

During the Occupy movement, some the non-news employees of the station would occasionally like to mock them, and tried to get the reporters to join in on it. I heard a lot of responses about journalistic integrity and needing to keep neutral, especially during a big story. One night some of the reporters were busy, so they asked me to rewrite some AP wire copy for a web article on Occupy. I was a little shocked when a few days later, someone commented accusing me of having an agenda for leaving out a detail not in the wire copy I was given. Simple rewrites of wire copy are a standard practice (but usually not the last word) for some stories, so take that for whatever it's worth.

I will say the news director is made to select stories to cover based on the station's demographic though, and it's definitely possible a preconceived notion of what they do or don't like could definitely negatively impact that. I did get to ask someone who used to be a news director outright if they ever canceled or modified a story because they didn't think a sponsor would like it. They said once, there was a scandal involving a sponsor, and some of the reporters started wondering if that would happen, but it never did in her career.

Anyway, just my $0.02. There's definitely problems with the news industry, but there's also a lot of hard working people at local stations who try their best to do things right. Don't write them off as Fox or CBS wannabes without listening/fact checking their stories first.

"An informal fallacy is an argument whose stated premises may fail to adequately support its proposed conclusion. The problem with an informal fallacy often stems from reasoning that renders the conclusion unpersuasive. In contrast to a formal fallacy of deduction, the error is not a flaw in logic."
Only referencing the list of logical fallacies in an argument an Appeal to Authority.

While I understand your reasoning, I can't agree with it. Appeal to authority is about borrowed legitimacy. While logical fallacies are generally standardized and taught in philosophy classes, they are logically derived, rather than being 'handed down from the mount'.

I think it's more correct to think of listing fallacies as a shorthand, a common frame of reference for those trained in formal logic to communicate succinctly. The logical falicies could be explained in full and do not require an authority's endorsement, but 'ad hominem' or 'straw man' are a quick and easy way to point to the flaw.

I agree, and understand. I'm in the math field, so I get not wanting to have to re-derive a principal every time you need to use it. My biggest issue with them is that pseudo-intellectuals, with no formal logical training, have attached on to them and use them to invalidate arguments at a whim. Logical falicies are really better used as rules to craft your own argument, than to find fault in others.

For example, the laws of thermodynamic say that entropy must always decrease. If I'm designing a system and I see a huge drop in entropy I know my math is probably wrong. However ,someone who has studied thermo knows that you can have a decrease in entropy if you have a greater increase somewhere else in the system. If you're just mindlessly asserting rules without knowing their nuance, then you are appealing to authority. I'm not talking about people who know this stuff and use it correctly, I'm talking about the people who are telling me a refrigerator won't work, because entropy decreases on the inside of it, neglecting that it increases even more outside of it. If you don't understand the derivation of these things and are tiring to shoe horn them into conversations, you are appealing to something you don't really understand.

Logical fallacies are indicators to look further into an augment, not ignore it.
